input: The affinity laws provide a convenient means of predicting how the performance of a centrifugal pump will change when the speed at which it is run is altered, and they are widely used for this purpose. The laws take the form of three proportionalities. The first of these states that the flow delivered by the pump is proportional to the speed, so that, if the speed is doubled, the flow is doubled as well, with the other conditions following the same change of speed. The second states that the head developed by the pump is proportional to the square of the speed, which means that the head rises considerably more steeply than the flow as the speed is increased. The third states that the power absorbed by the pump is proportional to the cube of the speed, and it is this relationship that tends to dominate the practical consequences of a change of speed. By way of a worked check on the third law, it may be noted that doubling the speed multiplies the power by 8, since the cube of the doubling factor is eight, a result that illustrates just how sensitive the power requirement is to even a modest change in operating speed. It should be borne in mind, however, that the laws are proportionalities for one and the same pump running at a changed speed on the same liquid, and that they rest on the assumption that the efficiency of the pump is unchanged, which is an approximation rather than an exact statement. They do not, strictly speaking, provide a means of transferring performance figures from one pump to another of a different design, and where they are applied, the figures they give should be understood as estimates that follow from the change of speed alone, with the behaviour of the system into which the pump delivers left to be considered separately.
target: The affinity laws state how the flow, head and power of a centrifugal pump change when its speed changes. The laws are three proportionalities. Flow is proportional to speed: at twice the speed, the pump delivers twice the flow, with the other conditions following the same change of speed. Head is proportional to the square of the speed, so the head rises more steeply than the flow as speed increases. Power is proportional to the cube of the speed, and the power change is the largest of the three for any given change of speed. A worked check on the power law makes the size of the change concrete. Doubling the speed multiplies the power by 8, because the cube of the doubling factor is eight. The check runs in the other direction as well: a pump slowed to half speed absorbs a small fraction of its former power, which is the reason speed control is used to trim a pump's output where the duty allows it. The laws are proportionalities for one pump at a changed speed, on the same liquid. Their basis is that the flow pattern inside the pump is preserved when the speed changes, and the derivation takes the efficiency as unchanged. Efficiency is not exactly unchanged in practice, so the laws give estimates, not exact predictions, and the error grows where the speed change is large. The laws also do not transfer a performance figure from one pump to another: a different impeller or casing has its own proportions, and the proportionalities follow from the geometry of the one machine being preserved. What the laws settle is the effect of speed alone. The head the system requires at the new flow is a separate question, answered by the system, not by the pump laws.
